perOption.reason: 'the defining skill that alone proves musical response' — reading: tapping need not be seen as the ONLY proof of musical response, and 'in fact my dogs responded to other musical features' seems to confirm it. Genuinely pulls via forward cohesion with 'musical features.' But it imports a framing the passage never sets up: the debate is whether ANIMALS are CAPABLE of responding to rhythm/music, not about what 'proves' musicality or which skill 'defines' it. Tapping is presented as a human behavior, never as evidence/proof of musical response. This makes the option orthogonal to the actual argument — an attractive but slightly foreign framing.

'proof that animals never react to any pronounced rhythm.' Directly echoes the established thesis 'it is wrong to claim that animals are incapable of responding to pronounced rhythms' (verbatim 'pronounced rhythm'). Concession-counter reads cleanly: deliberate rhythm-marking is uniquely human, BUT that human-uniqueness does not prove animals lack rhythmic responsiveness — the dogs demonstrably reacted to the jingling rhythm. 'In fact ... other musical features' then escalates the evidence beyond rhythm. Engages the passage's actual debate, no imported framing, no logical flaw.

'a trait unique only to dogs among nonhuman animals' contradicts the sentence itself, which calls tapping 'a particularly HUMAN skill,' not a dog trait. Pure word-association with 'dogs' elsewhere in the passage. Nonsensical: tapping is not something dogs do.

'merely a sign that an instrument is out of tune' lifts 'out of tune' from the closing Darwin example but has no logical link to the blank sentence about tapping being a human skill. Incoherent in context.

'the sole form of marking external rhythm by tapping' is circular/tautological — tapping being the sole form of marking rhythm by tapping is self-referential and empty. The passage never debates whether tapping is the 'sole form' of rhythm-marking, so denying it adds nothing and does not connect to the animal-musicality point.

note: Blank = concession-counter after conceding deliberate rhythm-marking (tapping) is uniquely human. Real contest is 1 vs 2. Option 2 wins on: (a) verbatim lexical echo of 'pronounced rhythm' from the earlier thesis, (b) direct reaffirmation of the passage's established claim that animals CAN respond to rhythm, (c) engaging the actual debate (animal capability) rather than an imported epistemic framing. Option 1 is the strongest trap — its forward echo with 'other musical features' is seductive — but it rests on a 'what proves musical response' framing the passage never establishes; hence rejected, though the residual pull keeps confidence at medium rather than high. Options 3/4/5 are shallow word-association or tautological distractors.
